content: Understanding the scope of the participant’s responsibilities involves comprehending the full extent of their immunization-related activities and the specific tasks these entail. To determine what contributes to the success of childhood immunization in a specific area, participants are asked to share their experiences regarding what helps families stay up to date with their children’s vaccinations. This question is intentionally broad and open-ended to capture a wide range of responses. Participants are also asked to identify the challenges they face in providing childhood immunizations in their area. For example: Are there difficulties with children falling behind on the vaccination schedule? Can you describe these challenges in detail? Are there issues with parents refusing vaccines for their children? Are you able to overcome these challenges? This line of questioning aims to identify and understand the barriers families face in keeping up with vaccinations within the participant’s jurisdiction. Participants are then asked what they would do to improve the childhood immunization situation in their area if given the opportunity. This question seeks to uncover additional issues or suggestions not previously addressed and serves as a closing question. The tools provided for assessing behavioral and social drivers of vaccination include a qualitative framework analysis template for caregivers, health workers, community influencers, and program managers. This framework is available in an Excel template to facilitate the interpretation of qualitative results. The analysis approach is not linear and is designed to support human-centered design for tailoring immunization programs. The BeSD COVID-19 Vaccination Survey is a globally standardized tool for assessing the drivers of COVID-19 vaccination. It includes 22 questions and is intended for completion by adults and health workers. When the full survey cannot be used, priority indicators should at least be measured. The survey includes a consent script and socio-demographic questions, which can be adapted as needed, but the core survey questions should remain unchanged. The survey measures various constructs, including: Confidence in the benefits of the COVID-19 vaccine: Participants are asked how important they believe getting a COVID-19 vaccine is for their health. The percentage of adults or health workers who consider the vaccine moderately or very important is recorded. Social processes, such as family norms: Participants are asked if most of their close family and friends want them to get a COVID-19 vaccine. The percentage of those who agree is measured. Motivation, such as the intention to get vaccinated: Participants are asked if they want to receive a COVID-19 vaccine. The percentage of those who express willingness is recorded. Practical issues, such as knowing where to get vaccinated: Participants are asked if they know where to go to get a COVID-19 vaccine. The percentage of those who know is measured. Affordability: Participants are asked how easy it is to pay for COVID-19 vaccination, considering clinic fees, transportation costs, and time away from work. The percentage of those who find it moderately or very easy to pay is recorded. The survey also includes questions about chronic conditions, previous COVID-19 diagnoses, perceived risk of contracting COVID-19, and vaccine uptake. For example: Participants are asked if they have a chronic condition, such as obesity, diabetes, or lung disease, to assess their priority for vaccination. They are asked if they have ever had COVID-19, and if so, whether it was mild or severe and confirmed by a test. This helps stratify data on vaccination intentions. Participants are asked how concerned they are about getting COVID-19 to assess their perceived risk. They are asked if they have received a COVID-19 vaccine and, if so, how many doses. This measures vaccine uptake. Additional questions assess confidence in the safety of the COVID-19 vaccine, trust in health workers administering the vaccine, and whether getting vaccinated would allow participants to safely see family and friends again. These questions aim to identify motivators and barriers to vaccination. The survey also collects demographic information, such as age, gender, and occupation, to enable stratified analysis. For example: Age is collected in completed years to allow analysis by age group. Gender identity is collected to enable stratified analysis and can include a third-gender option where culturally appropriate. Occupation is collected to identify health workers and essential service workers, allowing analysis by occupational group. The survey includes administrative questions for interviewers to record the date, participant ID, location, and area type (rural or urban). These questions ensure comparability and tracking and may be adapted to suit the survey methodology. Trained interviewers are instructed to read the survey questions and response options aloud to respondents, emphasizing underlined words and avoiding reading instructions in square brackets or all capitals. This ensures consistency and clarity in data collection.
